blocks.x: Let me jump in.
Get your name on here, the very first thing. Bob Watts. And is that your full name?
No, my full name is Robert Franklin Watts.
Robert Franklin Watts. See, the day is May the... This is February 28th. I mean February 28th, 1963. Let's get your name on here too since you'll probably be helping him out.
Alfred Williams.

And my name is Dick Allen. I think he's picking us up all right now. And where are we anyway? What's the address? 418 North Prairie. North Prairie. And this is your home where you're living now. But you knew each other somewhere else before. I know, we played together because he showed me pictures of it.
Oh yeah, in El Paso.
But let's start off at the beginning. Where were you born? New Orleans. Do you mind telling your birth date exactly?
Oh, 1907. February 17th.
February 17th. Well you didn't have a birth date too long ago.
That's right. That's right.
And exactly where were you born? What part of New Orleans? Or a town. Or a town. Let me see. Or do you know where you grew up anyway?
I think it was on Palmyra Street. Palmyra near Roman. Mm-hmm.
That must have had some music going on around there, some kind or another. Singing a music that you heard when you were young.

Well, my dad and my uncle. They was, you might say, my inspiration to start a musical career. What did they do? Well, they was tumblers, professional troopers traveling on the R.K. O. Sakers, you know, all over the country. See, they had acrobatic act. And of course my daddy, the final of the act would be my daddy would blow his trombone, and my uncle his trumpet and they'd play port and peasant, a duet, to close the act up after they got done tumbling. See, when the act was completed. They used that for final, see, closing.
Did they play alone or were the people in the pettacomps, or what?
Well, yes, they'd give them a little background. You know harmony on the, you know. Yeah. Yeah, see.
Did you ever hear of Wilton Crowley?
Wilton Crowley.

He was a clarinet player from, well, I, he played around New York. What he used to do is, he was a contorsionist, he played the clarinet while he was turning all around and everything, you know. I just wanted, they didn't do anything like that. They would stand up straight when they were playing around.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, perfectly straight.
They were trained musicians, or did they strictly run by head?

Oh no, they were strictly musicians. Yeah. And I used to tell them that I wanted to play something, see, but I hadn't made up my mind. But my daddy told me if I wanted to play, you know, following his footsteps, the trombone, I liked my uncle the trumpet, that he didn't want no ear playing, he was strictly against that, because they was musicians. He told me he was going to buy a book if I wanted one of them, that trumpet, and I had to study, and study hard. And he wanted me to study first. He wouldn't give me no instrument. He said, you study. You had to know it first. Yeah, you study, you know, your notes, you know the rudiments of it. Before you put your hand on it. Yeah, before you touch that trumpet, see. But no, nothing didn't come of that at that time. So I told him, I said, well I think I like the drum. And he went off on his tour, and maybe about a month or so after that, here come the Express company out there with a whole lot of big boxes. And that was my drum he sent from Chicago. See. So I started fooling around with the drum, see. But while I was fooling around, see, he wasn't, he didn't care if I used the ear on the drum, but he didn't want that on the trumpet, see. But I was playing around there, just beating all out in the yard. I'd go out in the yard and you couldn't see nothing but dust in the backyard, me and them drums, see. It's beating, man, because they found out I wanted to play drums by them old washtubs out in the yard. Because my mama, I kept them with holes in them. She just beat them, you know, out in the yard. And that's where they first found out that they better start, you know, give me the drums, and then, well finally they come back to town, they had some new material, as I said before, to their act. And then I started working with them. You understand, not on the circuit or KO, see, but you know, we'd practice at night, after dinner, every night. He and my uncle would play them duets, see, and then I'd get my drum set up there and it showed me how to work with them, you know. See, not too loud, you know, just to swing, you know, and play marches, whatever they wanted to play. See, they played some popular music, but they didn't play nothing by air. See, I had the air, see. I see. And I just was musically inclined, you might say, see.
How old were you when you first got the drums? Eight years.

Eight years old? Eight years old. Eight years old, yeah. And I think I played it about five years. With Gabriel. With who? Give me his name. Gabriel, you know, he was a trumpet player. Old man, Manuel Gabriel. Yeah, I think that was his name, yeah. And I was so small, see, I couldn't tell him I'm going to play with him. See, I tell him, you come on home and ask mom, and if she says it's alright, that's alright with me because I like to play with a band, see. So he come home and got my mother's permission, and then he had to carry the drum, and he didn't mind it at all. And I worked all on the boats out there on the lake, you know, in the summertime excursions, and on the train, he, I remember, excursions was poplin' in, see, going up the line there, you know, we'd play on the train and play when we got off at some pavilion somewhere. And then he, I remember back on Canal Street there, and big homes, he played a lot of house parties. They just liked him. He played a lot of house parties. I remember that clearly. Let's give a check on him here. I don't want to pay back.
But, I wanted to ask you about the very first job you ever went out on, whether you made money or not.
Who were you with?
Do you remember who you were with, or what it was?
Well, that was when I was playing drum with Gabriel. With Gabriel.
The first job you made money, you didn't do any playing just for fun.

Oh no, no, no. I was pretty good. What did y'all pay? Oh, I think around them times, you were five or six dollars a night, that was it. That was good. Eight to four. Yeah, oh yeah. That must have been good pay. Oh yeah, it was good. Oh yeah, yeah. But he didn't have his five pieces, but he used to get the good money. Yeah.
That was big pay.
Yeah, he was strictly, he was strictly-
The guy played in District Hall, knife a dollar quarter.

That's right. He played in District Hall, knife a dollar quarter. That's right. He played in District Hall, knife a dollar quarter. That's right. That's right. That's right. Five dollars, man, that's plenty of money. Yeah, you're so right.
Who did he have with him? Well, I don't remember the side man now.
I don't quite recollect where he was back there that far, see. No. What year that was it? About? Well, I was eight years old. I'm 56 now. Mm-hmm. See. Yeah, about 1950. What would that be?
About 50.
By 1950, honestly.
You were born in 1970 or 1980.
That's right.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Roughly so. Naturally, you wouldn't remember those guys. Sometimes those things stick in your mind the very first time you do something. Yeah, yeah. But I will never forget him because he gave me my foot break. Oh yeah. That's why I never forget old man, man.
I don't remember him.
I don't remember him. I don't remember him.
I don't remember him. I don't remember him. I don't remember him.
I don't remember him. I don't remember him. I don't remember him because he gave me my foot break. Oh yeah. That's why I never forget old man, Manu. Oh.
Manuel Gabriel. Just like you never forget your first girlfriend with all the others.
Yeah, yeah. Oh man, how you sound.
But, no, and you stayed with him quite a while on the drums then?

Well, I'd say about, I'd say about five years. I never worked with anyone else but him as a drummer. See? And then, shortly after that, my dad, they came back home to visit us. And whenever they come home off the road, they usually stay about two months. See? That's the only time our family saw our father and uncle, see? And they had new material. And then I told him, I said, these drums too coversome. I said, old man Manuel, when he gets through at night, he didn't have no case. He had a little bit of con cornet I remember. And he'd just put it in the bag and zip it up, put it on his arm in the wintertime, put his hand in his coat, so I can go on home. See? At least, but he had to carry my drum. But I noticed that, see? And I said, now if I keep on with these drums, when I get large enough, well I'm going to have to carry them all the time. That's right. I said, man, your hand's going to be out there in the wintertime, man, you, plenty of times, they ain't too hot about letting you get on the streetcars at that time with too much of that stuff, you know. That's never permitted. That's never permitted. Yeah, you see? So I told my daddy, see, after they returned, I said, well, I don't want no drums no more. I didn't want to practice no more with him. I can turn it off.
Let's see now. We were talking about, you played on excursions, boats you say, huh, some too, when you were playing drums even. And excursion trains.

Oh, and the trains? Trains, yeah, not the boat. How did that work then? Oh, well, you'd go down the railroad station, and different clubs used to use the train to go up the new road, different picnic areas, you know, baton roads, you know, and when you get there they'd get off, you know, and they always had some place that, you know, old pavilion like, you know, and they'd get off and you'd stay there all day and picnic, you see, but you'd be blowing, see. Now we played on the train going, you know, right on the train while they were going. What part of the train? The baggage car. Oh yeah.
In the baggage car.
Yeah, in the baggage car.
I see. Well, what did they do on the train to, did they pay money to get there in the first place to get tickets or? Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
They had to pay.
It was about two dollars round trip, yeah. Did they sell drinks or have gambling on the train or what? Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Beer? Sure. I had beer on the train. That's right. In tubs. In tubs, I see.
That's right.
That's right.
That's right. That's right.
That's right.
That's right. That's right. Yeah. But they had everything, man. Every Sunday. They got there they was ready for anything.
They had a squirtion every Sunday. And every. And every. Yeah. I see.

So they could make it pay that way. That's right. They made it on the ticket and. That's right. That's right. They even had them to Chicago. Used to play for Andrew Foster. Oh yeah. A guy named Andrew Foster used to give his good in Chicago. He got up there to stay. Uh huh. Went on the street to jump the job. We'd come back.
Uh huh.
1928. That's right. Guy Kelly.
If he just left on his own, you know. That's right. That's how they got it. Oh, Guy Kelly. Guy Kelly. Fine.
Fine. That's right. Yeah. I remember that. 1928. That's how they got to Chicago. Fine. They stayed. Uh huh. I guess that life got them both.
They must have lived too fast.

Yeah. Well they did. Lee admitted he lived too fast. Yeah. He drank too much. Water glasses of whiskey, you know. Yeah. And he'd come out cold nights like I done without overcoat and caught cold. You see. Uh huh. Give him cancer to love.
Oh, you were gonna help us cap with that. Yes, indeed.

Yeah. Well, uh, let me see. We were talking about the excursions and all that. Did you, uh, listen to other musicians besides your uncle and your father? I didn't get that name. That's right too. What's your father?
Uh, Joe Watts. My dad, his name was Joe Watts. Yeah. And my uncle was Lou Watts. Some people say Lou Watts.
Mm-hmm.

And, see, for years I guess, oh, before I was born, see, they was on the road, see, with this acrobat act, see. Mm-hmm. They even taught the great Gaines brothers of this city. They used to have a trucking company hauling trash and junk. Mm-hmm. But my daddy and them taught them. And then they went on the road to make a big name for themselves, see. Mm-hmm. But my daddy taught them right in the backyard on Palmyre Street. Mm-hmm. They had a wide yard there and they'd lay down the canvas first and then put that huge mat that they tumbled on. Mm-hmm. And they taught the Gaines brothers right there. I was very small but I was right there in the way. I see.
Yeah. But did you listen to the other musicians besides your father and your uncle much around?
Oh, yeah. Yeah. Back in my neighborhood, see, after we moved, see, we moved from Palmyre Street, see, up on Roman and Perdita.
Mm-hmm.
And then I used to be quite a fan of, well, even though Rainey was down on Iberville Street, he was the first man that ever got me in the Union, see.
Oh, I see.

See, but Rainey and then old Georgia Boyd lived right in the block not far from me on Perdita Street, right around the corner. See, I was on Roman between Badita and Perdita and George Boyd was right up. But who did you want to play like? Did you like Rene? Satchmo. You like Lewis? Lewis. That's after I put the drums down and got the trumpet. And when I got me some chops together, see, well, my mother had a combination, RCA Victor, a combination, and I'd buy everything. Now, I hung out at Morris Music Shop, he was a personal friend of mine, see, on Ramport Street. And I'd get everything Lewis made. At that time, he was bringing out Hebe Jebe's and Savoy when he had the hot Savoy 5 with Johnny Sensi and Dodds and all them old fellas, them real ones, see, real jazz aces. Oh, yeah. Well, I'd get every record he put out and put it on that thing and I'd time it just right. And I'd play note for note. And when I'd go to set in around these places, well, they didn't care too much for me to play. Because the music that they was playing, see, I don't care if they was playing stocks. When you played that stock, you played something Lewis played. Yeah, you see. When I took that chorus, I played it just like Lewis had recorded it. That's right. You understand? And they played like they liked me, all right. I had quite a lot of friends, but two men of them, they wouldn't want me to set in. You used to call him Little Lully. See? Yeah. Little Lully Armstrong. That's what I was known by for a long time and I was proud to be able to dig a little of Satchmo because he gave me the inspiration for the trumpet, even though I asked my uncle. My uncle wasn't nowhere around that kind of playing, you understand, that I wanted to do. Even when I asked them for that trumpet, I done heard Lully down there on Rampart Street, I stand out. Before I got chummy with old Morris, with old Morris Music Shop, I stand out there and listen at them speakers. And they had, each record they played, they're hanging the artist's picture out, see? And I dig Lully. I said, oh, I want to blow something like that. I want to blow something like that. And Lully was blowing then.
But you knew Lully before he left?
No, I met him when he came back. I see. You see, when Lully came back and played at the, what's that club up from, Club Forest? No, no.
Suboivin Garden? Suboivin Garden.

Suboivin Garden. 31. Yeah, you see. Well, he came back, well I had moved off Roma Street and I was living back in the block where John Casimir lived on Padida, between Johnson, I think, and Galvis. My family moved. And John, when Lully was out there, I had him to dedicate a couple of numbers to my mother, because they know that I was so crazy about him, copying his records all, you know, the whole time I was home, that's all I was doing. See, never got tired of blowing. See? And John Casimir, he'd come by my house and I had a porch, and that's the first I met him. He was a stranger when I first moved in the block. I didn't know nothing about John Casimir. And he come there and I'd be right in the front room there playing with that record, see? And then when I quit playing, I'd hear somebody clapping and I'd go through the screen door, I'd say, who's that out there? John said, that's fine, Gates, that's fine. And that's how I met John Casimir. And we've been friends ever since I could remember in my musical career. We've been very good, close friends. Now how did you get to go away? Well, I tell you, this is funny now. Back off Adidas Street, between Johnson and Priya, they had a little speakeasy. There was a house in the front, and you go through the alley and you come to the back, it had two big rooms. You know, sort of a little get-together joint, but they were selling that 15-cent white lightning. You know, 15 cents a half a pint. Yeah, if you can swallow it, brother, you're going to feel it if you can keep it down. And myself, you know, a little young drummer at the time, Lang, I don't know his first name. Lang, he come up with H.M. on and myself.
Fred ain't Lang the piano player now.
He's playing piano now, but he used to be the drummer. I don't know Lang. He played piano. Fred Lang.
Yeah, Fred Lang.
You don't know Lang?
He's an old-timer.
Lang.
L.M.G. L.M.G.
Yeah.
He's probably doing that, but I can't remember his name. He's one of them old-timers, too. I didn't catch him. He'd catch him around busters, you know. Oh, yeah?

Well, he was playing drums. This man's going to give us two dollars a night in this joint, three pieces. Had old beat-up piano back in the corner, one of them old uprights, you know. And Lang would sit on my right side. I'd sit on top the old upright, take the front out, and I'd sit on top, just beat the side of it. Me and my cornet, I had a con cornet. And I'm trying to think of the piano player. This boy was burnt pretty bad when he was a child. And his daddy used to pedal fruit on a wagon. They used to live on Johnson Street that near Tulane. And I can't think of that boy, but he burnt all over the face. But he could play, oh man, he could play. Anything I wanted to play a little bit, he had it, too. You understand? By ear, strictly by ear. And we called ourselves the Unholy Three. And man, we rocked that place, man. We didn't know what it was to take a break. Because at that time, see, I didn't smoke or take a drink. Until I was 25 years old, I made that promise to Mother. Because she told me, she said, I hate to see you trying to blow that horn, because you'll get out here with these other fellas, and you'll kill yourself drinking that old white lightning too early. But I made a promise, and I kept that promise. I put the first cigarette in my mouth when I was 25, and I took my first drink of that old white lightning. But now when I first took that drink, I wasn't drinking at this place where we was playing now, see. Well, the job lasted about six months. See, not every night. Friday, Saturday, and Sunday nights. How much a night? Two dollars a night. Two dollars a night. And that was big money for us. Eight to four. And I'd run right home and give it to Mama. I had my clothes, everything, but I just loved to help my mother. And she'd say, well, son, what do you want out of this? I said, oh, let me have a dollar. It's all right. Because I wasn't drinking. I wasn't smoking. I didn't need it, see. You know, I had my clothes. But eight to four, man, in that place, you couldn't see, sometimes you couldn't see the people dancing for the smoke.
You understand?

In six months, and it was some colored fellow. He'd run the place, but I done forgot his name. But he paid off. Every night he paid off. And I said, don't tell us now to wait till Saturday. That was the little MG, man. I said, don't let me wait till Saturday. If you can't pay tonight, man, you can't pay it when it doubles up. So you drop it on us every night, six bucks. Old man, on drums, and this boy playing a lot of piano. But when I pick up, some gonna get right there with that rhythm, man. That's probably three. Yeah, that one, Holy Three, was a loo-loo, man. Well, I worked there after that six months was over. No, while I was there, it was some fellas come from Fogway, and one of the saxophone players was named Milligan, John Milligan. And the other one was named Baker. Baker come from Crowley, Louisiana. Well, they was working with a band. They had a lot of- What's up, Baker? Yeah, Baker. And they was working with a man. They had a good job in Fogway, but they needed a trumpet player. And they come down here in a big, at that time, a big 1930 Master 6 Buick. And it was almost new. And they had the right talk, man. I mean, they really looked- Nice unit. You know, could impress you, you know. And they dug this joint. I didn't know how they found me. I knew nothing about them. And so one night, we were just going to town by 11 o'clock, man. They saw some fellas standing around a long time, you know. So after we got done playing, then Baker come up. He's the one who introduces us. And after we were formally acquainted, he said, what? He said, would you be interested in going back to Fullwood with us? I said, Fullwood? I said, man, where's that at? I ain't never left New Orleans. I didn't know there had no other place in our town than New Orleans, man. I said, where is that at? In Texas.
I said, where over there?

I said, oh, I don't know. I don't know, man. I don't know. I said, I'd have to talk to my mother about that. And I said, what's the deal? He said, well, we get $30 a week. He said, playing at a nice place. He said, we got a long-term contract. If you'd be interested, say, we've been around them many places and talked to many trumpet players, but we would prefer to have you, because you fit more with the band. And now, man, I fell right in it when I fell in with them, because they liked, you know, for a man to be featured. Because Baker, he played a lot of sax. And he'd feature, you know. Oh yes, he blowed a lot of sax, man. Like Coleman Hawkins, he had to use a mic with that tenor, because he was soft. But when you let him get by that mic, man, he was just like Coleman Hawkins. Big girl. And Bob Milliken was an alto player, but he was loud. He didn't need no mic. Rough. You understand? He was one of them rough players. But I mean, they played all that load. They know just how to make that harmony and everything. And they liked the men to be featured, see. And they said that they had been around many places, but out of all the trumpet players they talked to, they would like to get used. Yeah, you would fit in. You see, because I would fit in with their band, see. They called it their style. Yeah, you see. Oh, they must have had about eight pieces. And so, I told them, I said, well, you'd have to talk to my mom, I don't know, and I ain't made up my mind yet. So them fellas hung around here, man, and they come back to that place three straight nights, trying to get me to make up my mind. So I had talked to my mother in between, you see. And I told them, I said, well, I'll tell you what you do. Well, I think that was on a Tuesday night, the last time they came. I said, now you come by Wednesday evening. I give them my address. I said, I'm right down on Padilla Street. I said, you come by there and I want you to talk to Mama. And you explained it to her just how it is. I said, because I've never been away from here. I said, and she'll have to give it okay. What she say is all right with me. So they say, okay. So at 2 or 2.30, they were right at my door there. So I invited them in the house. I said, come on in. And then I called Mama from the kitchen. She was cooking there. I said, now Mama, I said, these boys want me to go away to four and play with them. I said, now they've got a good job over there. I said, now I believe I'd like to play with them. I said, but it's up to you. I said, because I ain't never been away that far before. See, I thought it was Plum and Nelly, man, you know, one of them strictly New Orleans, you know, catch, you know, just round, yeah. So she listened at them, he talked, and that big car out there might be a brand new. And man, they had the uniforms. You know, see, you know they didn't come in raggedy, because I'd have been scared, see. They had to tell them, say, if you need any loot, say, just what you need.
You thought it was Plum and Nelly?
Yeah, you know, yeah, man. I ain't never been away, man. I never thought I could leave away from here. Well, we went up on the job, man.
And what does Plum and Nelly mean? Some people don't know.

Well, that's just too far, man, when you ain't been there. Plum and Nelly up in Kip. Yeah, yeah, that's just too far when you ain't been there, see. You used that to praise your watchers. Not realize, you know, that you can cross Louisiana and go into Texas and just step across there. But a person that's never left New Orleans, you know, see, man, that's full way, that's way away from here. Oh, yeah. Well, I went on up there, and the job lasted pretty good for four months. See, they had a contract modified signed by the Notre Republic, too. But this man, he run away with all the money one night. One Saturday night, went away with all of them. We didn't get paid for that last week. And I don't know if he ever come back. Yeah, the boss. He went away, just left. Nobody in the way. And his wife said that she couldn't afford to carry that burden, because she didn't like that kind of business, no way. But he wanted to be in it. What was the name of the journey? Oh, similar to the one you had here, Dew Drop, you know. Oh, mm-hmm. Yeah. You know, we were drawing good crowds, man. I liked that band.
Did you get a teacher on trumpet when you did take it out?

Well, yeah. Well, my teacher was Henry Red Allen. Mm-hmm. See, at the time he was playing with Fate Marbles on the steamer capital. See? Well, he let me come over to his house, and nobody else wouldn't go over there and wake him up in the evening but me, twice a week. And I'd go over there, he never charged me nothing. And then I went and took two or three lessons. I paid 35 cents apiece for the lesson from Manuel Manetti.
He taught me too. Oh, yeah?

Yeah? Well, that's the man that really caught over my eyes about the music, see, because Henry Red Allen, he'd get over there and he'd be teaching me something. I kept my little book, you know, I had Otto Langs. I never forget his trumpet method. And Henry, he'd teach me a little something in there, and then he'd know that I liked the blow show, and then he'd put on a little records. He'd get there with his trumpet. And I'd get mine. Oh, yeah, he was like Dipper. And me and him would copy records. Well, I didn't get much musical education right there, but I got a lot, I mean, to learn by ear, see. And you can say what you want about these musicians coming up nowadays. It's good to get that music, my friend. But it's equally good to train your ear, because... The light might go out. Yeah, that's my kind of music, musicianship, man. You don't go all playing on no truck or playing in the dark. You ain't nowhere. So I'm glad I learnt my trumpet first before I fool with any music. You know what I mean? I'd advise any trumpet player to do the same. Fool with your horn first. Copy some star that you like. Copy the records. And then go get your music. Because it's not as hard as if you knew music, then you tried to get there. Too many of them tried it. They can't play nothing unless they got it wrote in front of them. And I never cared to be that kind of musician.

You know, P. Ron used to tell Arthur Durbny, Leo Dejan when he was playing on the boat with Dirty Pope, he used to tell them, say, man, why don't you put that music on the side? Try to memorize the music. Yeah. He was just looking at the music all the time. I suppose the lights go out. Yeah, that's right. And you know what happened? You see? And we was in the middle of a tune.
He said, now, didn't I tell you that? No, you can't play nothing. What happened, Gay? You can't play nothing. No, you see? The music automatically stopped.
Elliot Taylor, Arthur Durbny, Elliot Taylor, Arthur Durbny, and who else? Three of them. And Joe Ruzon.
Uh-huh. Joe Phillips. Uh-huh. Joe Phillips and Leo.
Uh-huh.
Joe Phillips was a tom, you see? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Joe Phillips would pick up something and play. And then, you know, it would be a little bit of a play.
Yeah. It would be a little bit of a play. Yeah. Oh, I like, I like that.
And we kept it going. But them fellas, I couldn't play nothing.
No. I couldn't play Peter Hunter. I told you that.
See that?
No, no. They just couldn't play my ear?
Couldn't play. Couldn't play nothing. Just home sweet home. Just couldn't play. I knew that. Elliot Taylor, Arthur Durbny, and Joe Luzin.
Couldn't take much. What was that?
He and Eddie, Alan Greta, Joe Phillips, the bass player, who we had on get ourselves.
So we kept it going.

And Jimmy John, Simon was on bass. It's time to take him sick. Then we got a guy out of St. Louis, Jimmy, Jimmy Jones. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And I mean, them guys couldn't play. Peter Hunter, I told you. You know what happened? Set them David Horn on the left. He stayed out in the hour. Yeah.
He went on to say, huh?
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Nice fine musician. Oh, yeah.
He'd talk it on down for you. He's a fine musician.
Yeah. Yeah. Musicianship. He said a teacher taught him two years before he let him pick up his violin. Wouldn't let him touch it.
