That's why they cut all that stuff out when the guys playing them bands.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. And them kind of fellas, like Will Hines and them and them guys from Chicago, New York, they think, you know, New Orleans musicians ain't nothing they can't read. Yeah. And Louis played his way and showed them that he could read. Oh yeah. All that gang, you know. Joe Oliver, Johnny Dodge, see? Yeah. Punch now, there wasn't no classification like that. No, that's what I'm saying. And he come up there and try to, Guy Kelly went up there and played with him. Oh, Guy was telling him. Guy could cheat and Guy could blow. That's right. Guy Kelly told him, say, man, put your music up there. That's right. I'm a little high, I say, but put your music up there. I heard what you done punched the other man.
Yeah.
Say, but you ain't gonna do me that. Uh-huh. Say, put your music up there.
That's right.
Well, I said, oh man, we ain't. That's right.
That's right. I said, put your music up there.
That's right. He'll cut everything on there. He'll put their music up there.
If it's fly specs on there, he going to play that.

At least a guy told him to play the first chorus down and got off and took it to their key to their Put your music up. That's right. Well, I told him, man, we ain't. I said, put your music up there, man. That's right. He'll cut it. He'll cut everything on there. He'll put that music up there.
If it's fly specs on there, he gonna play that.
At least they got to it up. Played the first scores down and got off and tore, split them up. Then they all wanted to play with him.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. And don't forget my little teacher now, Henry Red Allen.
Oh, yeah.
He sees specs, too, and he blow.
But let me tell you why he didn't make much of a reputation, what I heard, from musicians, you know.
Yeah.
He said he tried to imitate Lewis too much. Well, he did. You see, that's why he didn't make a reputation like Lewis.
He didn't try to work in a style of his own, you see.
He was copying, you see.
Yeah, yeah.

So that's what one of the musicians... Too much repetition. Yeah, that's what one of the boys come out there with Duke, you see. Yeah, yeah. He told me, I said, how come Alan ain't got on the top like Lewis? He said, well, he imitated Lewis. Yeah, yeah. He said he should have a style of his own. Then he said he played nice trumpet, playing the trumpet. Oh, yeah.
But he said he imitated. Too much.
Well, that's why I always did bring in my little gut bucket style with Lewis.

You know, I Lewis, if I'm playing a number, and I think about a couple of licks like Lewis would put in there. And if I want to, I put it in there. But I've got my own little gut bucket style. Yeah, most musicians do that. Like we used to work out in California. I used my own ideas, see.
Yeah, most musicians do that.

Because that's been gone. We used some of the licks, you know. Yeah. But that's been gone when I was young, when I was just, you know, just copping him, see. I made a name all through Texas, not only in y'all and I. At one time.
He's a good entertainer, man. Nice entertainer.

You see, at one time I come up right here. I'll tell you who come up. When Warline got a new Busha trumpet in, they sent me a card. They sent Sharky Banana a card. They sent Louis Primer a card at Warren Easton High School. We come up together. We'd go down there and get in a booth and get one of them sailmen to get on the piano. And we'd wake up with new trumpets. Now I'll come up with them fellas. Louis Primer went to Chicago. When I left, I went the wrong way to the wide open spaces of Texas. You understand? I could have been making records long time ago.
Wasn't nothing happening.
You understand, see? But ain't nothing happened where I went. But Primer, he went to Chicago. And Sharky, of course, you know, he's quite noted himself for that Dixieland music is controlling.
Well, he was making it down here in the 20s making records.
Yes, he was. Yes, he was. You remember that high society he recorded in that trumpet solo he played? Yeah. Oh, yeah, man. Oh, shocker, but none. Oh, lefty.
Yeah, I know.
And when I come back out to home in 45, Alfred, he was at the hurricane, I think on Frenchman. Hurricane. Hurricane. What was that club over there on Frenchman Street?
I wasn't here, man.
And it was all in tux. He had six pieces, but strictly gambling joint right in town on Frenchman.
By the river.
Yeah. No. By the river. Back then, no. I was on Turo. I was on Turo in, let's see, Claymore. By the Turo in between Johnson and Priya. I was living on Turo.
They got a bar in there now, Gail, tell me. Yeah, but two or three blocks down. On Priya.
Oh, yeah.
Some people stay by the house right there. Yeah. They got a bar right on that corner. They got everything in there.
Maybe so, but this was two or three blocks down on Frenchman. See, big, big, big club there, the Hurricane.
No.
And Sharky was playing in there.
I don't know where he's coming to.
You know where he is? Legionfield. Well, maybe so. Legionfield. Maybe so.

Legionfield between Durbin and Roman. Yeah. That's where, I remember that just as good. That's where it was on Legionfield. Yeah. Well, that's where Sharky was working. Because I used to walk up there and visit him some night. They had a police. Yeah. Used to be detailed. There used to be detailed at the economy hall. Uh-huh. And he told me how they had to knock down and drag out. Yeah. They closed up the joint, you know. Oh, yeah. Used to fight too much.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
A guy named Moirline. That's what Pogge said.
Uh-huh.
He said he wasn't no kid to them Moirline.
Well, I went there, man,
to talk about a beautiful place in town.

People informal. And here Sharky and this man in tux, man. Uh-huh. And just nothing but gambling tables. Long ball, gambling table. And now they'd be up at the ball. They'd be drinking a while. Now and then they played music. I never saw nobody on the ballroom floor, but the music was to draw the people, I guess, see. And now and then Sharky and Emma get up there. Come on, watch. Sit on the bandstand. I go up there and sit down and listen at him play a few numbers. And he was pretty ageable then, in 45. But I mean he could still blow.
Huh?
Blind?
Sharky? No, he's coming back now. He had something.
Diabetes. Oh, what?
Something, I forget. He was sick for a while, but he's coming back.
Oh, really? I heard he was going blind. Diabetes. Sure enough.
He had it, but no, he's playing this month.
Playing. Diabetes?
I think the 10th or something he's playing at the Royal Orleans.
Oh, yeah?

That's nice. You know, the Jazz Club is putting on a series of concerts. I think they've got Celestan and Paul Crawford's band. I got a postcard about it. I can't remember. They had a whole lineup of bands, a whole series of concerts. There's a little movement now to do a little something for it.
Oh, yeah. Well, who's carrying on Celestan's band since Papa's past?
Morris French's band.
Well, who's doing trumpet?
They've got Alvin Alcorn, though. Oh, that's right. They did.
Oh, Aja told me that, because I asked about Alvin.
Yeah, Alvin.
Yeah, see, Alvin's with them. Yeah. They play that Dixon man? Yeah. Oh, strictly Dixon man. Yeah.
Yeah, Fernandez used to play with him, Alvin Fernandez. Yeah, yeah, I remember Alvin.
What happened to him?
He played around.
Oh, is he? Uh-huh. That used to be Paul Barbaran, main man.
Does he play with Bob yet?
No, Howard's up there with Bob.
Oh, that's right.
They keep changing around, you know.
Kid Howard's with Bob.
Sometimes Kag is with Bob.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
It changes.
Uh-huh. Do that other boy be there? Used to play with him on his name, Pickett?
No, Pickett I haven't heard in...
That's who Bob really wants, you see. But I don't think he'll do it. That's who Bob really wants, Pickett, you see. Who? With a man like Howard, I heard. Oh, yeah. Yeah. See, that's what Bob won.
Pickett, did you find on Dixieland?
Actually, yeah, Bob musician. Oh, yeah? Uh-huh. He went away with Bob, nice musician.
Yeah. Well, let's see. He made that record with George. He doesn't use that George record. Brass Band record. No.
Album. Boy, it's all about fine. Uh-huh. Boy, that's a fine record. Uh-huh. You got a high five?
No, not yet. No, I'm back one of them old-time comedy. I get that record and send you. Yeah.
Boy, it's fine.
He was across the lake that day, huh? Uh-huh.
Across the lake.
No, no, I was sick. I had the flu just like I had. I've forgotten.
Yeah, I was sick.
It was a TV program you were across the lake on.
Yeah, a TV program.
That's right. Uh-huh. Every time something comes up. Ain't that something, I was gone. Yeah. Ain't that something?

Mine nearly broke home one time there. Yeah, I was with my little grandson. I fell down with him over the morning. Come up a rain. I fell. Well, the same old. And now the last time, about eight months ago, I went trying to knock the nickel down in the meter and broke this. Yeah, yeah. Charlie said, your bones is too dry. He said, you must do that. Get you old, will you? So you can't be hitting on nothing like that. This bone run nearby your first time? Right, right, right in there. Uh-huh. Yeah, right in there. Ooh, man, that's a funny. Uh-huh. I ain't never put a cast on there for eight weeks. Eight weeks.
Hmm.
I'm at a cop with, I think, in there.
Yeah, yeah, right in there. A little bone crack. He showed me the x-ray, but I couldn't read it. I didn't know what I was looking at.
The gate looked like we about to run out of here.
Yeah, it's indeed. We are.
I got more questions, too. Yeah, I don't know. We never did get it back to mute. She was saying you didn't fool with me so much. I accept.
No, but I. What's the problem? No.
When you were a kid, you didn't have one?
No.
I thought all corn cornets came with a mute or something.
Well, mine, mine.
Yeah, but a lot of them come with them, but they didn't use them.
Yeah. No, we didn't use them.
No, they didn't use them.
See, Joe I was using derby, see?
Yeah. He liked the derby, you see?
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, you see, that's what Joe liked. Then, late years, he started using his mute. But most of Joe and Buddy Betteen was derby, you see? Yeah. It gives a better effect, you know? Oh, yeah, yeah.
Not the ten derby, the real derby. The real, real derby.
No, the real derby gives you a better effect. The real, better effect. I had both since I was doing my musical career. Yeah, you had the ten derby. I had both of them, but that old.
Metal derby.
Metal derby. That metal derby don't give you the tone like that old. Felt. Felt derby. Oh. You get a lovely tone. Yes.
That's what Sharpie used, don't it? Old felt, don't it?
He wears it.
Yeah. Yeah. All the time. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
With a red fella. Yeah, old Sharpie. Nice trumpet player, man.
Oh, yeah.
I like Sharpie. That's a good one, man.
He used to blow like a song. Quote Tony Amarica, had another trumpet player around here. Bob Lord of Metty. Oh, yeah. Tony Amarica, he died last year.
Uh-huh.
Nice trumpet player. Yeah, I heard he died. Pass. Yeah, very nice, though. He died with cancer. Mm-hmm. Sure enough. Prostrate, I imagine.
Long time. Dying, too.
That's it. That's about it.
Mm-hmm.

This is Real 4 Bob Watts, February the 28th, 1963. There are some things I wanted to ask you about. I'll go right ahead. One thing, he showed me a picture of the band in 1941, Alfred did, in fact we got it up at school, with Melvin Wright and Jack Richards, a white talent player, and Martínez on piano. And did y'all have a guitar or a bass or anything in that band? There's a guy sitting on the stand and I can't see where his instruments.
No, no, we never used a bass. But sometime a bass player would come in and set in.
It couldn't have been a singer though, you had singers in the band.
And somebody was sitting up there by Alfred, the drummer?
I don't remember where he was sitting.
Well if he was sitting up there, that's a friend of ours on a big farm and ranch, that's Fred Scott. He used to come in quite often and sit up there and listen at his play.
I think it was a colored guy.
That could have been Fred Scott, yeah.
I just wondered, maybe Alfred will know. But you didn't use a bass.
No, we never had no bass, no guitar. Just piano and drum mostly.
You never did play any parades around here? When you came back from Fort Worth?
No, until I came back, until I was discharged out to Army.
Oh, until 1945?

45, not then. Then Alfred Williams, they heard that I was back here, you see. And I had been out there playing at George's, that's why I first got my greetings from Uncle Sam, see. Oh yeah. And I was just to be allowed to come to Shreeport because I had some people living in Shreeport. See. And at the time I had a girl that I was very fond of at that time, see, in Shreeport. So they gave me permission to go to Fort Humburg in Shreeport to be inducted, see. And so I cut on back down there to Shreeport. And then, after taking my examination and spending the night at the Veteran Hospital there for that spinal tap, well I was allowed, I was allowed to come to, at least to be fortunate enough to be sent home. Now at that time, before I got Norman, I was away from New Orleans for 12 years. See, well, they sent me home right to Camp Harahan, right out here in New Orleans. And usually they send me, you know, someone they inducted away from home to get them used to being away from his people, see. But they sent me right home for my basic training and I spent 17 weeks right out here in Camp Harahan taking my basics, see. But I didn't do any playing. I came out home in 45, I stayed a year around here. Oh, I played a few places. At that time the Foyne was running, that's the Jitney dance on Iberville Street there, between Ramport and Burgundy, the Foyne, and then they had another one, the La Vida. Well, Lee Collin was playing at the, I think, one or the other, the La Vida if I'm not mistaken, and Anderson, this boy who I played, who hires me every year to play this parade with his brass band, he was playing at the Foyne, or Vice Versus. And see, and Anderson would lay off a couple of nights a week because it was such a tough job, you know, the Jitney dance. And he let me work a couple of nights in his place. And then I used to go in some nights that I wasn't working, and I always like, Lee Collin's and I always been good friends. And I'd go in, as soon as I'd walk in, you know, he wanted to go down by the E-Light, you remember the old E-Light restaurant where the musicians used to gather on Ramport Street, he wanted to go down there and get a bite to eat, you know, about 10, 30, 11 o'clock.
What year was this?
Oh, that was around, when I was discharged, about 45, 45, 1945, that's when I was discharged. See, I wasn't in the Army in 43, see.
And Lee was back here, from Chicago.

Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. If he had went to Chicago he would show here, because he was playing right down there. Right next, you see the place, it was just two doors apart, see. One place, you go in, big ballroom way back there, and you go in this place, another nightclub, Foyne and the La Vita, see. And I used to go rest him up. He asked me how long I'm going to be there, I said, oh, I'll be here about an hour, but he said I'll walk around and stretch out a little. Yeah, he was here, most sure he was. That was the year, 45. Yeah. And then when I went, when I, when I, when I wrote to Alfred and them back in El Paso, because I always liked El Paso, because I wasn't messing up then like I did then, you know, before, you know, when I used to leave him sitting on the bandstand before I got in the Army, you know, and drinking, you know, food with that shawty, see, fighting shawty. Well, I wrote to Alfred, and then he, he wrote back, he was glad to hear from me, and said they would like to have me back out there. Well, I thought El Paso was going to be like it was before, you understand, because we used to make a lot of tips, you know, out at this California nightclub, see. Two weeks after soldier payday, it's mostly was a soldier house. You had to go by that, see. Two, two weeks after each payday, you make three and four dollars, we split up three and four dollars and quarters, nickels and dimes, you know, a tip a night, see. But at that time, George wasn't paying but about, oh, he wasn't paying but about seventeen dollars a week, see. But the tips used to them first two weeks, now the last two weeks of the month, soldier was, you know, getting rid of their loot and then it would really fall off, see. But I thought it was going to be like that, so I told him, yeah, I said, you send me a telegram, send me my ticket, I'll come on back out there. So I told my mother, the reason why I stayed here a year after I got out there from 45 to 46, way late in 46, because I hadn't seen my mother, been around her in twelve years, before they sent me right here to Harahan to take my training. Of course when I was in Harahan I'd come home every night and stay at my people's home, you see. And so I said I want to stay around my mom a while, so she asked me, she said, well, you've got to tell Graham to go back to El Paso, if you want to go, say, that's your living now. If it's a good job, you want to go, you just write to mom often, that's all right with mama. I said, well, all right, so I cut on back and went back out there, see. And then I played with Alfred, and well I done all right that time, I didn't mess up like that. And then it wasn't long after that that I met my wife, see. And then we was mad, and so I quit completely. And then the first opportunity that I had to come back from 45 was in 55, see. I came on to visit my wife all those years, I hadn't been back. But in 55 I brought my wife down to meet my folks, because they had heard I was married, and my people, if I must say so myself, is, well, my sisters are schoolteacher and one, own their own beauty shop, and they put it well up in society, you know. They want to see what they're born, I'm the only boy, I see, and three sisters. They want to see what I was going to bring back for a wife, see. And so I wanted them to meet my wife, because I knew that they would love her, and wish they do, see. They just idolize her, because they give her credit for stopping from drinking, because they used to hate for me to be around home, because they know I drink like that, and you know, it was always worth, mama was, my sister was, that something would happen to me. So I come back in 55. That's the first time I played for the Buzzards with Anderson. See, that's my first parade.

In 55? Yeah, 55. I must have seen you, you know. Yeah. I used to stay with the Zulus for a while there, but this year I thought I'd change it up, you know. And I caught all of them just about the same, up there. I didn't see the Corner Club.
No, you didn't see the Corner Club.
So you've been with the Buzzards every year, huh?

Yeah, in 55, and then I was able to come back again in 56. I played for the Buzzards again with Anderson, the same trumpet player, you know Anderson, don't you? Oh, yeah, I know. Yeah, well I played with him, see, again in 55 and 56. That's why I was surprised after seven years, when I come back this Mardi Gras, that he said that two or three years ago he had changed and went and started playing for the Lions Club, see. I thought we were still going to play for the Buzzards, you know. Of course it didn't make no difference, see, because I'm out there for the Lute anyway, I ain't feel that walking no more. But I, but like I can inform you right now, I'm 56 years old, and that is the last parade. Yeah, whenever I come, be fortunate enough to come back to visit my mother and my family. See, I will get on the truck or even in the ballroom, and if I don't, if I can't be booked in either one of those places, well then I'll just take Mardi Gras off and enjoy it with my wife, but no more walking. Right. From 730 to 430, that's a little too much, and for the money. Oh. See, your money, they don't pay you nothing. I want that to be down in history, in the records. They don't pay your thing for all that walking you do and blowing on top of it. You really got to blow out there. See, you can't get by on no crutch like you can in a hall where you got a sax to pick it
up.

See, there's three trumpets. When one takes down, the other one is blowing, the other one is blowing. And when you take a number down, you're all three blow. When you take that number out, you're all three blow.
And how long do you have in between numbers? They give you any time between numbers?

Well yeah, like the Lions Club used these two bands, see, where Broussard had his band up in the front, see, right behind some of the marches, you know. Roussard, Oscar Roussard. Yeah, he had his brass band. The Alphablan, yeah. Yeah. See, he was right behind a long column of, oh, they have a large club that lines. He was right behind some, then some old marches behind him, and then Anderson Band behind them, and then behind us, the remaining of the marches, see. Well, you would one band play a number, see, and they might play it maybe four or five blocks. I mean, they might play it a long time. But when that band takes down, the other one starts, see.
So that gave you a little right.

Yeah, well, yeah, yeah, but you're still walking. And then you can't hardly keep up, see, because the leaders, you know, see, they might keep you back, our band back a little bit, but that lets the front band, the front part of the parade get too far ahead of you. Then he wants you to tighten it up. Then you can, I'd almost get in a run to get straight again. When you get straight, he ought to keep you that distance, see. But you know they're walking along having fun drinking, you know. See, well, but still yet if you're not playing, you're walking, and that's where you feel it. See.
What about who was in the band with you?
Oh, no, Anderson.
Anderson, he always have a, some young fellas, you know, that I don't know, you know.
I didn't know the clarinet played.

No, no, neither did I. He didn't play it when I was in 45 and 56 with us. I think that's Anderson's young cousin. See, he's just starting out. And I didn't even know the other trumpet fella, Alfred knows him. But I did know the bass, the bass drummer in the snap drummer. Abbie Williams and the young mob. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Trombone player didn't show up. We had a trombone book.
Who was it?

I don't know what Anderson said. You know who he was? He said he was the distillery, Anderson said. Still on Howard Street. Yeah, he was the distillery. He ain't in the union. Oh, Buster. He was with the Zulus. Who was he, you see? You see that? See that.
See, he ain't in the union, and he got to pay that five dollars, you see. Oh, and the saxophone player that played with us, one of the saxophone players, had

a trombone player for him a week before Miley Graw. But Anderson said, well no, I didn't promise it to so and so. And the saxophone player said, you see, I could have got you a good man. But no, you said you had me. Well, there it is. What's that?
The Buster's a strong trombone player. Yeah, they're strong.
And ready, you know.
And playing with the Zulus, and stood Anderson up, in other words. Can you beat that?
I wonder how much they get. They say they get much of them. With the Zulus? Yeah.
And the Eureka got 32 or something, man, or something like that. Yeah. Four hours.
Oh yeah? Well, Zulus didn't go much longer than that. I don't know.
I'm about 11.30, so I left them.

Yeah, they didn't go much longer. Can you beat that? They come back up there and they went for it. Some people say they didn't go to Orleans Street, but the route, they say they had the route all messed up, you see. The route was in the paper wasn't like the route they'd taken.
You see.

The paper said they was going down Cleveland to St. Benard, then back up on the uptown side, St. Benard, to Portris, South Portris, to Simon Bolivar. Through those pass up right on up Simon Bolivar. To Jackson, back Jackson to Magnolia. Down Magnolia to Melton-Mead. Back out Melton-Mead and Simon Bolivar, this band. That's what I read, see. Yeah. But they say it was all together different.

They made it up, I think, more or less by the route, because I caught them on a cell in Ohio Street. They made their turn at Louisiana. That's where I rode with Louis Haney and Melvin Green in the captain's car. Because I remember that, and I remember getting into the car. I remember a good bit.
Well, they went to Luzon Avenue.
Yeah, and turned around on my cell, and that was what the paper said.
And come back down my cell.
Come back down my cell. And then I...
Went to where?

I got off from watching the Luzon Avenue on the bus. Oh, you don't know where then went. I was so tired then. But you know, that's what the paper said. They were doing it like that. That's what they said. But I guess they broke up.

Well, now we got 35 cents, man, for all day. Yeah. I mean, you trucked. The only break we got was at Padra Street. Mm-hmm. You know where they got that place that they eat and all? Yeah, I do. Yeah. That was, they let us stop there about an hour.
Mm-hmm. That's all.
And that's all from 7.30 to 4.30, because I kept the time right on them.
Well, it was before 7.30, just a little, huh? Oh, yeah.
When we started out? Mm-hmm. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Before 7.30. Oh, yeah.
I got that before 7.30 and I...

See, because I met them at Luzon and Ferret at 6.30. Mm-hmm. And Anderson wasn't long picking us up. And we hit right on out there to where they were farming at. See, what street was that? Who was it player for? Carson Noble, way out there in the Irish Channel. Who was it player for? Lions.
But it was up there, right by Alderman Park, Henry Clay, I think, when I called you.
Oh, that's where they left from, way up there. Yeah. Well, they didn't leave from the Lions Club. Mm-mm. The Lions is the Lion and Nance Asian.
Yeah, yeah. That's where we broke up at. That's where you broke up. Yeah. But no, they was further up in that gate.
Oh, yeah. About Alderman Park. Well, yeah, man. That's where they leave from. Buzzards and all that gate.

I never saw so much of St. Charles Avenue. Looked like I walked around the Belt before we hit Canal Street. Jesus, God. And when you get down to St. Charles, just like I told you before, both them bands is working. Mm-hmm. And I understood Anderson and Broussard. What? Say, now when we get there in front of all them people, the reviewing stand is just packed. Rex is reviewing stands all of them. Say, keep both them bands going. And we did that all the way down to St. Charles Canal and then turned Canal and kept both the bands going. He's playing different numbers. Soon they get down one number they pick up another one. And Tony went to the magazine and started back up. Lordy, I'm with you.
Paul Barber had the right idea with those five drummers, with that field band. You ain't no lie. Sure.
That was a risk. Sure, that's what gave you a break.
Sure, that's what gave you a break.
Sure, that's what gave you a break. He could work one snare drummer, you know, very easy.
Oh, sure, sure. And one bass drummer, they could split it up. That's right, that's right. He had the right idea. He sure did.
Three flat clarinet players, I'll never hear that again. Three.
You can think of my boy John Kazmaier.
He was a powerful man for a brass band.
When he get in it you're going to hear him. I don't care if he got three trumpets.
They made 45,000 from him that night. Yeah. He was a powerful man for a brass band. And when he get in it you're going to hear him. I don't care if he got three trumpets.

They made 45, Nelson told me that night. I don't know. That's what Nelson told me. I didn't know. I asked him for it. Who did he? Nelson did about right now. Oh yeah? 45. Can you beat that? They walked just one week. They walked one week. Can you beat that?

Pete was as happy as he could be. Yeah, they walked one week. And Charlie Weaver played Cornette with him, you know, the comedian. You didn't know, I didn't know that. He's on the Today Show or something. Is he? Yeah.
Not that, what is he? Charlie Weaver, the comedian?
Yeah, Cornette.
Can he play Cornette? He had it.
Sure enough. Old baggity-pants, please. Yeah, Charlie Weaver. I've seen him on many programs.
Jack Parr actually used to play. Yeah, he used to be often on Jack Parr. But he was playing on that thing. No, I've never seen him play nothing. No, but he was playing alone.
Sure enough.
He was just after trumpet. Can you beat that?
He and, alas, Jack was, because they were playing a duet and I couldn't hear it too good. I don't remember too well. I was a... He was high.
Well, I was tired. You was riding with Shorty? Yeah, he had Shorty.
I was, well I got up at 5.30, the same as you I guess. And, by that time that was 12.30, I was dead tired. Then I walked, you know. Oh, Jesus God. I caught four clubs.

What, you had your equipment? No. No, no, I was just walking. You were just walking. No, you were just walking. And you caught four clubs. Second clubs. You had to jump to catch them four clubs. Yeah.
Well, I did catch a little bus ride down then. That was moving, you know. And Ron, in case of the bus. You know, you're not going to catch him on the bus. No.
No.
You probably saw me, but you wouldn't recognize him. No, you wouldn't know that.
No. I had my costume. He was masked. Oh, uh-huh. The Mardi Gras. Yeah. The roles of the Mardi Gras.
Uh, listen, did your mother go to church? You were talking about her, you know, everything and drinking.

Your mother was a church worker? Oh, yeah. Yeah. Oh. But none of them could. Don't care how they prayed or what they did, they just, I guess I just, wasn't ready to quit. You didn't go to church yourself when you were young? Oh, yeah. What church was that? Oh, Wesley, Wesley Methodist Church upon David did.
Yeah. One of the oldest Methodist churches in the city. It is.
Wesley Church. Yeah. And what kind of singing did they do in the church? I just wondered, is it different from what they sing now in churches? No. No. No, no. No, no.
It's the same. Old-fashioned songs, old-fashioned religion. And then when they sing hymns like when I was a little dear to them. Yeah, yeah, sure.

What was some of the hymns? No, no, no. It's the same. Old fashioned songs, old fashioned religion. Yeah, it's the same. And they don't remember, they sing M's when I was a little player like that. Yeah, yeah, sure.
What was the other than M's?
Oh, Leaning, Leaning on Everlasting Arm.
Mm-hmm.
Oh, there was quite a, yeah, in this piece we played, swung on the parade the other day, by and by.
When the Morning Come.
All those old standards. The old standards, you know.
Yeah, standards.
But do they kind of give them that rhythm like the sanctified people and the Baptist people do?
No, no, no, it's a difference there. No, it's a difference there. Yeah, it's a difference. You get your real junk music from a holiness church.
Yeah, that's where the holiness is.
Because they put that in that beat. Yeah. That after beat, man. Yeah, you might hear a guitar up there. It puts it in a beat. Yeah, that after beat, man. Yeah, that after.
I heard a trumpet play the other night.
Yeah. What? What? You see?
Oh, you don't like that.
That must be for Reggie Josephine. You ought to go around there.
I've been there.
You been there? Yeah. I never saw a trumpet play.
No. No. No.
Well, I know one of the preachers.
Well, this must be up on Flake Street, eh? I don't know. You know they got a homeless church up there. Blake, that's up in Colton, eh? Well, I tell you now.
No, no, that's way down in Gentile. That's Mama Lou's church. Oh. Howard and Handy would play down there sometimes in the church.
Oh, huh.
Can you imagine John Handy playing on the church?
Yeah.
I think Handy's mother was Mother Richards in the church or something. Oh, I see.

Well, now, I, uh, when I was in Lorton, Oklahoma, I was in Lorton, Oklahoma on a job at the Rock Tavern there. I just remember what year it was, but anyway, I was with Henry Boyden's orchestra. We had seven pieces and we played every night except Sunday, I think. And we used to make trips up to Tulsa in Oklahoma City, see, you know, on our off nights, you know. And we was broadcasting them, 15 minutes every evening on the radio for this rock tavern, but we played, see, nightly. And I went, I visited a holiness church in Tulsa, Arizona that seats about, oh, about 1,500 people. And at that time, they had a spiritual crusade going on, a revival in other words. And man, them people had seven pizzas up there on that pulpit every night. And man, you talking about playing. I don't know where the fellas come from. I never met them. I don't know if they're from Louisiana or New Orleans or where, but them fellas really was playing them, swinging those spirituals.
Same as New Orleans style.

Yeah, you know, yeah, yeah. You know, for me not to recognize them as some of the old jazzmen, sidemen of the city, you know. They was really playing, man. I just got a kick just sitting there and just listening at them. And it's really to hear those hymns when they play it like that, you know. I see, Father. See, I'm telling you. That's why I always wanted to play a funeral and never have played when I'm 56 years old. Because I think when they're taking the body to the grave, ain't nothing could be sweeter than a brass band walking slow, playing those slow spirituals, you know.
I know.

Just so close, so walk with the, uh, Nero, My God, the D, and oh, they got some lovely numbers. Just barely walking. And each man playing his part, like the first trumpet, the second trumpet, like that. You know, getting all the harmony out of it, you know. Oh, that's the most beautiful thing. Because when I was a kid, I used to, man, I used to second line moldy band around here. Yeah. That's where I first met Kid Rainey. Uh-huh. Please.
He would play a lot of them, huh?
Huh?
He would play a lot of films.

Oh, man. Oh, yeah, man. That man had a tone on the trumpet, man. Like somebody just singing. Just so sweet. And his execution was so, oh, man, so perfect. Lurie tried to get him. Now, I do know that. Lurie tried to get him to come to Chicago after Lurie went up there and went over so big. But Rainey, he too stuck on New Orleans. And he couldn't stay out these corner bars. Now, he's another one like, you know, you know, like them old time musicians. They drank that stuff. They fought it too much, man. He'd have let it ruin the career. If he ever had any career, he'd have let it ruin him, you know. He was an old man. Chuck Lewis tried to send and had a place for him up there. You know, with another band, you know, but he could have made some big money. I don't want to leave them all. You don't want to leave them corner bars.
Yeah. What about, uh, who was your favorite brass band back then? Did you follow anyone in particular? Yeah.
I used to like the tuxedo. The original tuxedo. That's when Papa Celestan, the original tuxedo brass band.
You probably heard Lurie Armstrong or that and didn't even know him.

Yeah, I guess so. I was so little, you know, as soon as I hear a band, you know, our kids used to be, you know, I'd run out there and get on the sidewalk and I'd be with that long second line. But I think that's the one I can remember more, you know, that I followed. The tuxedo. And then there used to be the old Olympic. I don't know if they're still in existence, are they? No. Olympia. Because the Eureka, well, that's something that come up, that's just new to me when I come back home after the war. See, you know, and father, you know what I mean, in 55 when I come in and play it myself. That's the first time I heard of the Eureka. It's pretty old by and off. Yeah, I imagine it is. And my boy John Cadmey, he'd been with them, I think, for a long time, if I'm not mistaken. And you know, when I come in 55, and I came back in 56, well, Anderson had me sold up, because I always let Alfred know about three weeks before I come. And Anderson, he keeps in touch with him near Mardi Gras, about three weeks before Mardi Gras. Because if I'm coming, I'll let Alfred know, see? And I came in 56, and I met John Cadmey. He was playing with Eureka, and we was parading the buzzers, and we passed them somewhere uptown there. And John waved up and we were both taking a break at some place. John's band, he was coming this side street and we was on this street. Well we just stopped right there and we took a break. And John said, now Bob, if you ever come back, he said, you ain't never played with me. He said, why don't you play with me? Let me know one time. Play with me one congo. I said, well all right, the next time I come, John, I'll let you know.
He had the young tuxedo, John. I think Tillman's got it now since he died.
Tillman has taken off all the jobs. Oh, Tillman, uh-huh, yeah, I know Tillman. His cousin.
His cousin, yeah.
Yeah, yeah, I know Tillman, yeah. That is his cousin, sure is.
Who was your favorite clarinet player back in those days? Did you have a favorite? Oh yeah.
Well I'll tell you, my favorite clarinet player is, he's around here right now, and that's George. Lewis.
George Lewis, huh?
Yeah.
Who was he with in those times?

Well I don't know. George would look like he was freelancing, you know. He'd play with, you know, just so many of them, but he was always so popular, so busy, you know. Yeah. He had another tall brownskin fellow, I don't know his name. He played fine clarinet for brass band work. But George Lewis, see I made a couple of jobs with him years ago, see, playing at a hall, a ballroom, see, back on the main street between Claiborne and, what is that? San Jacinto. San Jacinto. Yeah, I had the privilege of playing with George Lewis. He hired me with his little combo, see. Now that was, that was before I left New Orleans, that was in 45, see, when I was home visiting my people. When I stayed here that year, you know, after I got out of the army, I made a couple of jobs with George Lewis back there. But to sit down and listen at clarinet players, I tell you that old George Lewis, man, he used to, I mean, old George Lewis from back there with that old bad cough, that strong cough, it sounded like his lungs coming out, no blood or nothing. He used to blow a lot of clarinet. Who's this? Old George Lewis. George Lewis, the one that's living now, yeah. No, no.
You mean George A. Boyd?
George A. Boyd, that's who I mean. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, not George Lewis, George A. Boyd.
So you liked both of them, huh?
Yes, I did. Oh, yeah.
I wonder who the tall, brown-skinned boy in the street was that you heard on clarinet that was good?
I don't know, I might know his name, but I can't. Who did he play with?
You don't remember what band?

Oh, he played with the Eureka, played a while with the Eureka. And in 55 when I come here with Anderson, he played for the Buzzy with us, he was Anderson's clarinet player. Yeah. And I can't think of that fella's name, tall fella, brown-skinned, and blows a lot of clarinet. No E-flat, B-flat. You use that B-flat.
The only one I can think of maybe is Brother Cornbread or something like that, but that doesn't sound right. No, I can't remember.
No. I forget.
I have to look it up.
I have to look it up. Yeah, good problem to have it. Somewhat. Because he's one of the old side men, he's really one of the old druner here. And I haven't seen him this year, I don't know maybe.
What about drummers in the old days? Since you played the old drums, who did you listen to then?
I used to like Happies. Which one? Well that goes back to the Lyric Theater, Roboshaw's orchestra.
Red Happy or Black Happy?

Red Happy, Red Happy. Well I like Happy on the drum, but the brass band too. I think the old two Happies was my favorite. Happy was favorite for that orchestra, that pit boy in the theater, and Lil Black Happy on that street. He was a little, little son. He was a showman.
On the snare? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Did you listen to many bass drum players?
Oh yeah, oh yeah.
Who did you like on the bass drum right then?
Well now, I'll tell you one thing, this man played with us, Connival, is now he might get somebody to play as good as him, but now you ain't gonna find nobody.
Name him up.
Yeah, you ain't gonna find nobody now to, to play that bass like he does with that enthusiasm.
Yeah.
You know, such enthusiasm, you know. See now they had a good one up in the Bruton band, Bill Phillips. He's pretty good with that. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Opening of the interview at Watts's home, with Alfred Williams present
segments.summary: Names, date (28 Feb 1963) and address are put on tape; Alfred Williams, Watts's former El Paso bandleader, sits in.

segments.title: Watts's birth in 1907 and the Palmyra Street neighborhood
segments.summary: Born in New Orleans on 17 February 1907, near Palmyra and Roman Streets; asked about music around the house.

segments.title: Father and uncle, acrobats and brass players, and getting his first drum
segments.summary: His father (trombone) and uncle (trumpet) toured vaudeville with an acrobatic act and closed it with a duet; his father insisted on study before a trumpet, so Watts took the drum and rehearsed with them.

segments.title: Playing drums as a boy with Manuel Gabriel and the first paid job
segments.summary: At eight he began on drums with old cornetist Manuel Gabriel, played excursions and house parties, and earned five or six dollars a night; he credits Gabriel with his start.

segments.title: Giving up the drums because he had to be carried around
segments.summary: After about five years on drums, Watts tells his father he is tired of the drums and the carrying, and wants to stop.

segments.title: Excursion trains: playing in the baggage car to picnic pavilions
segments.summary: Clubs hired bands for Sunday train excursions to picnic grounds; the band played in the baggage car, tickets were about two dollars, and beer was sold in tubs.

segments.title: Alfred on Andrew Foster, Guy Kelly and musicians who went to Chicago and lived too fast
segments.summary: Alfred recalls friends who left for Chicago in 1928 and who drank heavily and died young.

segments.title: Joe and Lou Watts, and teaching the Gaines brothers to tumble
segments.summary: Watts names his father Joe and uncle Lou Watts, who taught the Gaines brothers acrobatics in their Palmyra Street backyard.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: The Roman Street neighborhood, Rainey, and copying Louis Armstrong records
segments.summary: After the family moved, he lived near Kid Rena and George Boyd; he bought every Armstrong record from a Rampart Street music shop and copied them note for note, earning the name Little Louis.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: Meeting Armstrong on his return and befriending John Casimir
segments.summary: Watts met Armstrong when he came back to New Orleans, and met John Casimir when Casimir heard him playing along with records from a front porch.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: The Unholy Three in a Johnson Street speakeasy
segments.summary: Playing cornet in a three-piece band at two dollars a night, Watts kept a promise to his mother not to drink or smoke until he was 25, and tells of the speakeasy's paymaster.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: Recruited by a Texas band and leaving New Orleans for the first time
segments.summary: Saxophonists Milligan and Baker, with a big Buick and uniforms, offer $30 a week in Texas; he gets his mother's approval, goes, and the boss runs off with a week's pay after four months.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: Trumpet lessons from Henry Red Allen and Manuel Manetta, and learning by ear
segments.summary: Red Allen taught him informally twice a week and Manetta gave 35-cent lessons; Watts argues for learning to copy records before learning to read.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: Alfred's story of the lights going out on the boat band
segments.summary: Alfred tells how the Piron boat band's players, who read only from music, could not play when the lights went out, naming those who could not play by ear.

segments.chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
segments.title: Strict teachers: no touching the instrument until the notes are learned
segments.summary: Alfred and Watts compare teachers who held back the instrument for two years; Watts's father bought him the Otto Langey method book before the horn.

segments.title: Reel 2 begins with Alfred on saxophone players in his California band
segments.summary: On a new reel, Allen asks Alfred about saxophonists such as Red Spikes who played in his California band.

segments.title: Arriving in El Paso: Tiny Joe, George Alexander and the California nightclub
segments.summary: Watts reaches El Paso, works four or five months with a band, and describes the booker Tiny Joe and George Alexander's California club, where tips equalled salary and fights broke out beside the bar.

segments.title: Leaving the California for Hobbs, New Mexico, and the Ramona's racketeer owner
segments.summary: After a year as MC with a new group, Watts goes to Hobbs and finds the Ramona nightclub controlled by oilman and slot-machine racketeer Cecil Thompson.

segments.title: Jitney dance work at the Ramona with Tommy Brooks
segments.summary: Watts rejoins Tommy Brooks's nine-piece band playing for ticket-a-dance hostesses; he explains the rotating thirty-minute breaks and the nine-to-six Saturday nights.

segments.title: Drinking on the bandstand and the oil-field setting at the Ramona
segments.summary: Musicians bought their own drinks except a free fifth from the owner at 11 o'clock; Watts says he sipped carefully, and describes the oil-field smell.

segments.title: The Tokyo Club with McQueen: floor shows and reading the acts
segments.summary: Watts moves to Alice McQueen's band at the Tokyo Club, where his reading ability handled floor-show music, and a small Dixieland group played in the ballroom between sets.

segments.chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
segments.title: Alfred recalls being hired for the Ruidoso summer resort in 1936
segments.summary: Alfred tells at length how Mr. Clayton and his partner hired his five-piece band for a summer resort in the New Mexico mountains, negotiating the pay up, and describes the band and a bear in camp.

segments.chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
segments.title: Ruidoso summer, the white band from Dallas, and the band visiting Watts's dance
segments.summary: Alfred tells of playing for a white resort crowd who treated the Black band royally, and of going to Watts's dance in Central, where Watts played all the Louis Armstrong records.

segments.chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
segments.title: Saxophonists in El Paso: Melvin and Lacey Wright, Roland, and arranger Russell McGatts
segments.summary: They recall Melvin Wright's death, the alto player Roland at the Chinese Garden, the Wright brothers' arranging, and the trumpeter Russell McGatts.

segments.chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
segments.title: Working with Boots and his Buddies in San Antonio
segments.summary: Watts worked four months with Boots in San Antonio until the bandleader's trouble with young Mexican girls, then returned to El Paso.

segments.chapter: Alfred Williams and the Ruidoso summer
segments.title: Alfred sends for Watts in 1946
segments.summary: Alfred, in New Orleans to marry off his daughter, asks to hire Watts for his El Paso band despite his reputation as a drinker.

segments.title: Shorty: musicians' name for whiskey, and Watts playing high at the California
segments.summary: Watts and Alfred explain that Shorty means liquor and tell of Watts coming to work at George's club drunk.

segments.title: Alfred's story of the Saturday night confrontation over 12th Street Rag
segments.summary: Alfred tells how Watts, drunk, taunted him on the bandstand and challenged the band to play 12th Street Rag.

segments.title: Fired for the last time after eight chances
segments.summary: The boss George ordered Watts out after he caused trouble again and Alfred had taken him back eight times; Alfred replaced him with a Mexican trumpeter.

segments.title: The Mexican trumpeter who followed Watts and his marijuana arrest
segments.summary: They discuss the Mexican player who left for Los Angeles, who played blues-style trumpet and could not read, and who was arrested for marijuana.

segments.title: How Watts gave up drinking when he married
segments.summary: Watts tells how his future wife, a church worker, told him that either she or the whiskey must go, and he quit sixteen years earlier.

segments.title: Alfred never drunk in ten years; New Orleans musicians then and now
segments.summary: Alfred notes his dependability, and Allen remarks that he rarely sees New Orleans musicians drunk on the job nowadays.

segments.title: Hard-drinking old New Orleans players: Kid Punch, Chris Kelly and others
segments.summary: They recall older musicians who drank heavily, naming Chris Kelly, Kid Punch Miller, Yank Johnson and others, and Punch's cough.

segments.title: Watts not asked to sit in on his visit to a New Orleans club
segments.summary: On a Mardi Gras visit Watts sat in a club for half an hour; a musician said he would try to find him work, but nobody dared invite him up.

segments.title: Sit-in policies and drunken players on the bandstand
segments.summary: They discuss why bands stopped letting musicians sit in, including drunk players and reading music, and trumpeters seeking Shorty.

segments.title: Punch Miller humiliated by the Earl Hines band at the Grand Terrace
segments.summary: Alfred tells how Hines's men walked off the stand when Punch could not read the music, and how Guy Kelly insisted on seeing the music.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Henry Red Allen's imitation of Armstrong and why he did not rise
segments.summary: Watts and Alfred agree Red Allen was a fine player but copied Louis too closely, which they believe limited his reputation.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Watts's own gut-bucket style apart from Armstrong
segments.summary: Watts says he took a few Armstrong licks but developed his own gut-bucket style, and made a name across Texas.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Coming up with Sharkey Bonano and Louis Prima
segments.summary: Watts recalls getting trumpet cards with Sharkey Bonano and Louis Prima, who succeeded while he went to Texas; Allen mentions Sharkey's 1920s records.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Sharkey Bonano at the Hurricane club in 1945, and his recent illness
segments.summary: Watts remembers the Hurricane, a gambling club on Frenchman Street, where Sharkey played, and they argue about the location.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Present-day bands: Celestin's band, Alvin Alcorn and Kid Howard
segments.summary: They discuss who now leads Celestin's band, trumpeters in Paul Barbarin's and other bands, the Jazz Club concerts and a George Boyd brass band record.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Chatter about a TV program, Alfred's broken arm, and the tape running out
segments.summary: Brief talk about a TV program, Alfred's cracked arm, and noting that the tape is about to run out.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Mutes: derby, felt and metal, and not having one as a boy
segments.summary: They discuss mutes, with Watts saying he had none as a child and that a felt derby gives a better tone than a metal one.

segments.chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
segments.title: Trumpeters Sharpie and Tony Almerico
segments.summary: They comment on trumpeter Sharpie Jones's felt derby and on Tony Almerico, who died of cancer the previous year.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: The 1941 band photograph and who sat in the band
segments.summary: Allen asks about a 1941 photo of Alfred's El Paso band; Watts says they used no bass or guitar, mostly piano and drums.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Induction into the Army and a year at home after discharge
segments.summary: Watts was inducted at Shreveport, did basic training at Camp Harahan in New Orleans, and after discharge worked a few nights at jitney dance halls.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Returning to El Paso, meeting his wife and first return to New Orleans
segments.summary: After a year with his mother, Watts rejoins Alfred in El Paso, meets his wife and quits drinking; he returns to New Orleans in 1955 for his first Mardi Gras parade.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Marching with Anderson's Buzzards band, and pay for Mardi Gras
segments.summary: Watts played the Buzzards parade with Anderson in 1955 and 1956 and says 1963 will be his last, since the walking and playing is hard for little pay.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Two brass bands alternating in the Lions Club parade
segments.summary: Watts explains how Broussard's band and Anderson's alternated numbers, so players got a rest while still walking.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Anderson's band personnel, a missing trombonist and union dues
segments.summary: They discuss the young players in Anderson's band, a trombonist who left him for the Zulus, and what the Zulus and Eureka paid.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: The Zulu parade route as printed versus as marched
segments.summary: Alfred and Allen compare the route printed in the paper with the route the Zulu parade took.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: The Lions Club parade day: hours, pay and the St. Charles reviewing stand
segments.summary: Watts recounts the all-day march with one hour's break for 35 cents, from Luzon and Ferret to Canal Street.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Brass band instrumentation and drummers
segments.summary: They praise Paul Barbarin's use of multiple drummers and talk about clarinet and bass drum players in brass bands.

segments.chapter: Army, return to El Paso and Mardi Gras parades
segments.title: Takings, Charlie Weaver and exhausted Mardi Gras days
segments.summary: Nelson says the Zulus made 45 dollars, Allen mentions comedian Charlie Weaver playing cornet, and they trade stories of tiring parade day.

segments.title: Church music and singing in Watts's youth
segments.summary: Watts says his mother was a church worker and he attended Wesley Methodist; they discuss hymns and the holiness churches' beat.

segments.title: Trumpets in holiness churches and John Handy
segments.summary: Allen mentions trumpets heard in holiness churches, including Mama Lou's church where Howard and John Handy played.

segments.title: A Tulsa holiness revival and his wish to play a funeral
segments.summary: With Henry Boyden's orchestra at a Tulsa tavern, Watts heard a holiness band swing spirituals, and says he has never played a funeral.

segments.title: Kid Rena's tone and why he never left New Orleans
segments.summary: Watts remembers second lining behind Kid Rena, praises his sweet tone and says he stayed in the corner bars rather than join Armstrong in Chicago.

segments.title: Favorite brass bands: Tuxedo, Olympia and Eureka, and John Casimir
segments.summary: Watts followed the Tuxedo brass band as a boy, first heard the Eureka in 1955, and John Casimir invited him to play with him.

segments.title: Favorite clarinetists: George Lewis, George Boyd and a tall brown-skinned player
segments.summary: Watts names George Lewis and George Boyd, played a few jobs with Lewis in 1945, and cannot recall a tall clarinetist in the Eureka.

segments.title: Favorite drummers: the two Happys
segments.summary: As a drummer Watts liked Red Happy Bolton at the Lyric Theater and Black Happy Goldston in the street.

segments.title: Bass drummers, Connival and Bill Phillips
segments.summary: Watts praises Connival's enthusiasm on bass drum and mentions Bill Phillips in the Bruton band.
